summary:
Caquetá is a department of Colombia and stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition with no surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025.

Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. A couple presenting a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office is entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as a heterosexual spouse.

Access to public and commercial premises rests on Constitutional Court judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk). A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Within Caquetá, organised armed groups run a "social cleansing" campaign. Flyers distributed on the streets and via WhatsApp name "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, and further campaigns announce a cleansing of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots". A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night; a second trans woman said a friend of hers had been killed. Trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men. Discrimination limits trans women in the department mainly to hairdressing or sex work.

Lethal anti-trans violence is a national pattern that a visitor to Caquetá faces. On 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, 32, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia; the assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April, and she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents but no arrests followed even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and her mother Sandra Borja said: "They killed her for being who she was." Thirteen trans people were killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023, and eight trans women were killed between February and April 2024.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.
tangentialFactors:
Organised targeting is not confined to Caquetá. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case, described in reporting as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict.

The national legal framework and the security situation move in opposite directions. Colombia's recognition regime compares favourably with most of Latin America on paper, yet the May 2025 UN fact-finding mission found institutional progress disconnected from daily lived experience, and the July 2023 transitional-justice indictments rest on the state's own acknowledgment that conflict-driven violence against LGBTI people amounts to gender persecution.
localsOnly:
Trans Colombians handle document changes themselves: a signed declaration before a notary replaces the judicial route of bodily inspections and psychiatric assessments, and the same process applies to residents of Caquetá as to any other department. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree and the May 2018 executive decree bind national institutions on LGBTI rights in education, health care, prisons, victim services, housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Residents face the same employment ceiling as the wider trans population in the department, where discrimination confines most trans women to hairdressing or sex work, and the same flyer campaigns circulated on local streets and in WhatsApp groups. Domestic accountability runs through the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, which indicted 15 former rebels in July 2023 for crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities.
outOfScopeNotes: No source in this inventory gives Caquetá-specific homicide figures for trans people, nor records whether the "social cleansing" flyer campaigns in the department have led to arrests or prosecutions; both remain unresolved. Whether the November 2025 "trans" and "non-binary" identity markers are issued by Caquetá registration offices is not sourced here. The status of the comprehensive trans law under legislative consideration in 2025, and the number of arrests ultimately made in the Millerey case after the April 2025 reporting, are likewise unresolved in this inventory. Police capacity to protect individuals named on local kill lists is not addressed by any available source.
